title: Provide private vulnerability reporting and automated security maintenance
scope: Add a concise public SECURITY.md with a private reporting route and supported-version policy; enable GitHub private vulnerability reporting and Dependabot security updates for this repository. Configure bounded dependency-update coverage for app and app/mcp and review GitHub Actions update coverage and immutable action references. Preserve the owner-only merge and approval workflow; do not change main branch protections or release signing in this task.
acceptance: Visitors can find the security policy and open a private vulnerability report without filing a public issue; verify the reporting route and GitHub setting.
GitHub API confirms private vulnerability reporting and Dependabot security updates are enabled.

Dependabot configuration covers the two existing npm lockfiles and GitHub Actions with a bounded update schedule; validate the configuration and confirm security/update changes still require the repository's ordinary PR and owner-merge workflow.
Document and verify the chosen Actions dependency controls against the existing release workflows; existing required CI passes for any workflow changes.

values.goal: Maintain trusted local task operations for developers and AI agents using the public Outask AI distribution.
values.value: Users can disclose vulnerabilities privately and the owner receives automated dependency-remediation PRs.
values.observable_result: A usable private reporting route and enabled, verifiable automated security maintenance in the public repository.
values.verification: Inspect the public security policy/reporting route, GitHub security-setting API responses and update configuration; verify affected CI contracts.

notes: Requested as low priority after the repository audit. Observed: SECURITY.md absent, private vulnerability reporting disabled, Dependabot security updates disabled; dependency audits currently run in CI. Creating this task does not authorise implementation or remote-setting changes.

title: Publish SHA256SUMS for release archives
scope: Generate and publish a deterministic SHA256SUMS release asset containing SHA-256 checksums and exact filenames for the three accepted platform archives. Hash the final archives actually uploaded, without rebuilding them. Integrate the extra asset into release publication, retry/recovery validation and downloaded-archive acceptance, and provide concise Linux, macOS and Windows verification commands in the existing installation/release documentation. Preserve exact approved notes, existing published releases and Actions-owned publication.
acceptance: Each new release publishes SHA256SUMS with exactly one standard checksum entry for each of its Linux x64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 archives, using their final uploaded bytes and filenames.

Publication and recovery accept an identical existing checksum asset, upload only missing assets and reject mismatches; partial uploads cannot publish an incomplete or inconsistent release. Existing releases are not rewritten.
Native downloaded-release acceptance verifies each downloaded platform archive against the downloaded SHA256SUMS; a changed archive or invalid/missing checksum entry fails clearly.

Users can follow documented platform-specific verification commands successfully for a matching archive and observe a failure for altered bytes. Explain that checksums verify file integrity and are not a signature of origin.
Focused release-generation, publication and recovery checks plus required CI pass; actual publication/download results are verified read-only after an approved owner merge.

values.goal: Distribute usable and verifiable Outask AI CLI/MCP archives.
values.value: Users can check that their downloaded archive matches the bytes published for its release before installing.
values.observable_result: A downloadable checksum asset and working verification instructions for all three supported platforms.
values.verification: Compare SHA256SUMS with the actual published/downloaded archives and exercise matching and tampered-file verification scenarios.

notes: Requested by the owner after the release-integrity discussion. This task adds checksums, not signing, notarization or artifact attestations. Priority defaults to medium; only the separate security-maintenance task was explicitly requested as low.

title: Prevent cross-clone task ID collisions with optional shared ID allocation
scope: Add opt-in shared ID allocation for task creation while retaining numeric task IDs. Provide a minimal usable HTTP allocator with durable atomic per-project counters and integrate its reservation protocol into shared creation used by core/standalone, CLI and MCP. Configuration explicitly enables allocation and selects the service URL and stable project key shared across clones; absent/disabled configuration preserves local allocation and performs no network requests. The service reserves and returns an ID rather than merely exposing the last occupied ID. Define the minimal endpoint/configuration contract, service deployment route and authentication during technical design. Keep task records local JSON; the shared service holds only allocation state. This task must deliver a runnable allocator and working multi-clone creation, not just a client for an unspecified future backend.
acceptance: Without enabled shared allocation, existing creation behavior and interfaces remain compatible and make no allocator requests. Enabled configuration validates the endpoint and stable project key; local absolute paths are not used as cross-clone project identity.

Two independent clones configured for the same shared project can create tasks concurrently and receive distinct positive safe-integer IDs; project keys isolate counters. Allocation is an atomic durable reservation and survives service restart.

Provide an explicit safe enrollment procedure that starts above all existing IDs and retained counters across participating clones. Request floors cannot move the shared counter backward; adding an older/offline clone requires reconciliation. Clearly document that unconfigured/offline writers cannot share this uniqueness guarantee.

Retries after lost replies use the same allocation-request identity and cannot accidentally reserve a different ID for that retry. Failed local creation may leave a harmless reserved gap; IDs are not recycled. Allocation idempotency does not falsely claim whole-task-creation idempotency.

When enabled, unreachable/unauthorized service, timeouts, malformed replies, exhausted counters and locally conflicting returned IDs fail clearly without creating a task or silently falling back to local allocation. Explicit-ID creation must not bypass shared uniqueness; define and verify its reservation/rejection behavior.

Authentication credentials remain outside committed project records, request/response sizes and waits are bounded, and endpoint trust/HTTPS requirements are documented. Network waits do not hold the local writer lock; final local validation, blockers, collision checks and write coordination still run safely after reservation.

Exercise the actual runnable allocator and at least two independent project directories through shared creation and affected CLI/MCP boundaries, including concurrency, retry, restart, outage and disabled-mode scenarios. Keep transport behavior and public contracts aligned and pass required CI.

Document minimal service setup, opt-in configuration, safe enrollment, failure handling and the limitation that unique IDs do not automatically resolve Git merges of task JSON. Update the existing local-only product contract to describe the explicitly optional allocation-state service.

values.goal: Keep repository-local JSON tasks usable by developers and agents working in independent clones.
values.value: Participating clones can create tasks with globally distinct project-scoped numeric IDs without manual prefixing or renumbering.
values.observable_result: A runnable shared allocator and opt-in tracker configuration demonstrate concurrent task creation across independent clones without ID collisions.
values.verification: Run concurrent creates against one durable allocator from two separate project directories; verify distinct IDs before/after restart, safe retry/outage behavior and unchanged network-free local mode.

notes: Owner proposed an optional config-controlled address for querying the latest occupied project ID. Refined to atomic reservation because a read-last-then-increment protocol still races between clients.
Existing numeric IDs, blockers and references remain numeric; this task does not adopt composite per-person identifiers.

Choose the smallest deployable service/storage option during technical design. Do not assume a hosting provider or create paid infrastructure from this planning request. Task creation does not start implementation or deployment.

title: Simplify installer completion messages across platforms
scope: Update the packaged Linux, macOS and Windows installer messages and completion behavior. Remove all suggestions to close the window using keyboard shortcuts, including 'If the window stays open, close it with Cmd+W.'. Always display the short command 'tasks' in Command; retain the platform-appropriate full executable path with correct quoting in Run immediately for use before a new terminal is opened. End successful installation with 'Installation complete. Open a new terminal to start working.'. Append 'Press any key to finish.' and wait for a key only in launch contexts where the installer window would otherwise close automatically; omit both the prompt and wait when the terminal remains open. Preserve the installed-location line and readable spacing. This task covers completion messages and pause behavior, not update functionality.
acceptance: Successful installation shows 'Installed OutaskAI at <installation path>.', a blank line, 'Command: tasks', 'Run immediately: <correctly quoted full executable path> --help', a blank line, and 'Installation complete. Open a new terminal to start working.'.

macOS output uses the actual paths, for example: Installed OutaskAI at /Users/user/Library/Application Support/OutaskAI. followed by Command: tasks and Run immediately: '/Users/user/.local/bin/tasks' --help, with the agreed blank lines.
No installer message suggests closing the window with Cmd+W or another keyboard shortcut.
'Press any key to finish.' and its key wait are present only for launch contexts where the window otherwise closes automatically. Persistent terminal sessions show neither the prompt nor the wait.

Focused platform installer checks verify final output, short Command, executable-path quoting for paths containing spaces, and pause behavior in automatically closing windows versus persistent terminals; inspect captured successful installation output at the user boundary and run the applicable project gates.
values: Goal: provide usable packaged CLI/MCP installation on supported Linux, macOS and Windows platforms (docs/product.md). Value: users immediately see the short CLI command and a usable immediate-run command, without unnecessary window-closing instructions or key waits. Observable result: the completed installer presents the agreed concise message and pauses only when needed to keep an automatically closing window readable. Verification: inspect successful installer output and exit/pause behavior for automatically closing launches and persistent terminal sessions on the supported platform routes.

title: Unify Outask branding and installation paths with compatible command aliases
scope: Use Outask as the official displayed product name and outask as the canonical command and service identifier across CLI, MCP, read-only HTTP/API, installation and distribution entry points, help, documentation and agent instructions. Ship tasks and outaskai as permanent supported aliases using the same implementation and behavior. Preserve existing public entry points and integration/configuration compatibility without mandatory data migration. Where technically supported, running services launched through any alias identify and display themselves as outask; investigate and document concrete platform or client limitations. This is product naming, not a mechanical rename of the task domain: preserve task JSON fields, the tasks/ directory, domain operation names such as list_tasks and task resource routes unless an actual product-identity boundary requires a compatible alias. Keep current AI-development positioning in README content only. Use one permanent platform-specific Outask application directory, migrate existing managed installations safely and retire confirmed obsolete managed application copies without accumulating release directories. Complete uninstall of application-owned global configuration and caches remains task 12. Consolidate default global configuration, disposable SQLite caches and safely migrated coordination storage under the same Outask root. Inventory and minimize external command/PATH/profile/hook integrations, migrate confirmed legacy entries, and verify isolated lifecycle tests do not pollute the operator's real user directories. Audit old product identifiers through runtime, manifests, generated distribution artifacts and the complete release/update/recovery contract; retain only required compatibility spellings and task-domain names.
acceptance: Installed CLI exposes outask, tasks and outaskai without user-defined shell aliases. Equivalent invocations, including MCP startup, have matching arguments, operations, outputs, errors and exit codes. Both aliases are permanent, with no removal schedule or deprecation warnings.

The official displayed product name is Outask; outask is the canonical command and protocol/service identifier where lowercase identifiers are required. CLI help, command examples, continuation guidance, MCP/HTTP identity and current distribution/package/service branding use these names. AI-development positioning and the descriptive Outask AI/task-tracker wording belong only in README content. Preserve agreed permanent aliases and legacy installation/configuration recognition without presenting legacy names as the current brand.

Services started using outask, tasks or outaskai report the canonical identity outask in protocol metadata and service/process names controlled by the application where technically supported. Check actual running services; document any platform/client-controlled display limitation and its concrete reason without claiming universal OS process-name control.

Install, update, reinstall and uninstall support all three commands on the supported Linux x64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 distributions. Existing tasks-based installations upgrade successfully; aliases use the same installation and version and introduce no conflicting copies or leftover managed launchers.

Existing records, IDs, unknown JSON fields, task stores, schemas and supported configuration remain usable without mandatory migration. Task-domain names such as tasks JSON fields, tasks/ storage, list_tasks and task resource routes are not mechanically renamed.

Update owning documentation, setup examples and repository/agent instructions to use outask as canonical and explain permanent tasks/outaskai compatibility. Review branding references across CLI, MCP, API and release/installation surfaces while preserving historical facts.

Verify from the installed-product boundary: run representative CLI reads and help with all three names, connect an MCP client through each command and inspect server identity, and inspect the HTTP/API identity. Check alias parity and existing connection/configuration compatibility, plus affected native distribution install/update/uninstall acceptance and focused regression checks. Record actual evidence and any supported-platform limitations.

Fresh packaged installs use one permanent Outask root: ~/.local/share/outask on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/Outask on macOS, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Outask on Windows. Keep the default application-owned persistent footprint inside that root, including application files, disposable SQLite read caches (cache/), default global configuration (config.json) and writer-coordination files (locks/), subject to the safe coordination migration below. Do not create a releases layer or accumulate version-named application copies. Explicit user-selected external paths remain supported and must be inventoried; do not delete arbitrary external locations.

Upgrade existing tasks-based and OutaskAI installations and default global settings to the canonical root without losing project/skill records, user configuration, existing command integrations or unrelated files. Move or rebuild the disposable cache under the new root; old default ~/.cache/task-tracker and ~/.config/task-tracker paths must not remain active defaults. Retire confirmed obsolete managed application payloads, launchers and legacy integration blocks after successful migration, preserving user-owned content and stopping for resolution where ownership is uncertain. Verify fresh/migrated install, update rollback, repeated update and fresh CLI/MCP behavior through native distribution acceptance; remove temporary download/staging/rollback files after success.

Preserve one writer-coordination namespace across aliases, clients and differing cache/config/temp environment settings. Audit POSIX /var/tmp/task-tracker-locks-<uid> and Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\OutaskAI\locks separately from disposable caches. Do not delete or replace live SQLite lock files or silently split old/new writers between independent locks. Any lock-path change that is incompatible with existing writers must follow the documented coordination-protocol migration boundary, with active writes finished and affected old sessions closed before new writers start; do not claim ordinary live-session compatibility for such a change. Record any temporarily retained legacy lock location and the exact safe retirement condition.

Inventory persistent files and integrations outside the canonical root on Linux, macOS and Windows: POSIX command links in ~/.local/bin, shell PATH/profile blocks (including ZDOTDIR), Windows command-launcher directories and user PATH registry entries, explicitly configured global paths, and explicitly installed project Git hooks/client setup references. Keep only necessary external command/PATH integrations by default; repeated install/update must not add duplicate or temporary-path blocks. Update or remove only confirmed application-owned legacy integration entries while preserving unrelated profile/PATH/hook content and project/skill data. Full standard uninstall cleanup remains task 12.

Audit current naming across CLI help/version/runtime errors, MCP identity and argument descriptions, HTTP/API headers, package manifests/lockfiles, installer/help/PATH markers, generated archive directory/README/asset names, updater asset selection, release title recognition/publication/notes validation/recovery, agent guidance and tests. Current product branding must be Outask/outask; retain task-tracker/OutaskAI/TASK_TRACKER_CONFIG spellings only for necessary legacy recognition, agreed permanent aliases or historical compatibility fixtures. Update affected release contracts together, preserving already published tags/assets/approved historical notes. Keep task-domain operation/store names and project coordination/recovery filenames compatible rather than mechanically renaming them.

Run lifecycle and migration acceptance in isolated user/cache/config/temporary locations on all supported hosts. Verify that test installs, cache refreshes and teardown do not modify the operator's real shell profiles or global configuration, leave temporary-path PATH blocks, or retain test cache generations outside their owned fixture. Account for fixed writer-lock storage safely after test clients close. Verify the resulting installed footprint, not only renamed source literals.

values.goal: Outask: developers and local agents share repository-local task operations.
values.value: Give users one recognizable Outask product and one current installation, preserving existing command integrations.
values.observable_result: Users run the same Outask installation through all supported aliases, with default app/config/cache/state consolidated under one platform Outask root and necessary external integrations explicitly accounted for.
values.verification: Use all three installed commands for the same CLI operations and MCP startup, inspect CLI help and MCP/HTTP service identity, and verify upgrade compatibility and managed launcher lifecycle in supported distribution acceptance. Verify fresh and migrated platform installation paths, preserved user data and removal of confirmed obsolete managed application payloads. Inspect installed filesystem/profile/PATH footprint, legacy config/cache/lock migration safety and test isolation on the supported native platforms.

notes: Owner approved consolidating SQLite caches under ~/.local/share/outask as well as application files (corresponding platform Outask roots on macOS/Windows). Audit found additional defaults: ~/.config/task-tracker/config.json (or TASK_TRACKER_CONFIG/XDG override); ~/.cache/task-tracker/search/<project-path-hash>/{current.json,index-*.sqlite,refresh.sqlite}; POSIX /var/tmp/task-tracker-locks-<uid> and Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\OutaskAI\locks; POSIX ~/.local/bin launchers and shell profiles; Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\OutaskAI\bin plus user PATH; explicitly installed project pre-commit hooks. Cache refresh is disposable; writer coordination is not. docs/contract.md requires same-host/same-user fixed coordination independent of environment and a coordinated restart for incompatible protocol migration.

Read-only local footprint audit: ~/.config/task-tracker absent; ~/.cache/task-tracker contains 14422 files / 724048966 bytes; /var/tmp/task-tracker-locks-1000 contains 1725 zero-byte files; ~/.local/share/task-tracker retains the current OutaskAI installation plus old task-tracker-0.1.0-linux-x64. Both ~/.bashrc and ~/.profile contain 182 managed Outask PATH blocks: 181 referencing temporary paths and one local user-bin block. These are observed existing artifacts; no host cleanup or application changes were performed during this planning audit.

Naming scan (excluding dependencies/generated lockfile bodies): 25 runtime/build files, 11 documentation files and 28 test files contain legacy branding. Key owners: app/cli.mjs, app/runtime.cjs, app/http.mjs, app/mcp/server.mjs, app/{,mcp/}package.json, app/src/{config,search-index,project-lock,stores,service}.mjs, app/scripts/{install-launcher,install-path,install-cli,install-release,update-release,hook,release}.mjs, scripts/{release-config,release-pr,release-notes,release-recovery,release-upload,install-local-release}.mjs and docs/outask-ai-skill.md. Package lockfile root package names must follow manifest changes. Preserve project metadata/recovery contracts and historical release recognition.

title: Remove installed application files, global configuration and caches during uninstall
scope: Change the standard uninstall flow so removing Outask AI deletes the managed tasks command, installed application copies, application-owned global/user configuration and application caches, when present. Cover the supported packaged installers on Linux x64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 and the documented source-checkout uninstall route where applicable. Preserve task records and configuration inside projects and skills, source checkouts and unrelated user files. Update affected uninstall help, messages and documentation to describe the resulting behavior.
acceptance: For each supported installation/uninstall route, inventory the application-owned installation, global configuration and cache paths actually created or used, including configured locations, and make standard uninstall remove those artifacts together with the managed tasks command.

Verify an install -> use/configure -> uninstall scenario in an isolated user environment: installed application files, application-owned global configuration and any generated caches are absent afterward.
Verify project task records and configuration, configuration inside skills, source checkout contents and unrelated neighboring files remain unchanged after uninstall.
Verify uninstall succeeds when optional configuration or cache paths are absent and that existing protection against removing an unrelated command remains effective.

Update focused installer/distribution checks and uninstall help/documentation to reflect complete application cleanup and retained project/skill data; verify supported platform behavior through the project's native distribution gates.
values: Goal: keep project tasks in readable repository-local JSON usable without the tracker (docs/product.md). User value: uninstall leaves no installed application, global configuration or cache behind while retaining the user's project and skill data. Immediate observable result: a completed standard uninstall cleans the application-owned machine/user footprint. Verification: install and exercise Outask AI in an isolated user environment, uninstall it, assert the application-owned paths are absent and compare retained project/skill files with their pre-uninstall contents.

title: Add a Windows MSI distribution
scope: Add a usable MSI (.msi) distribution of Outask AI for Windows x64, alongside existing archives. Include reproducible packaging, release integration and concise platform-specific installation, update and removal instructions using the native Windows package installer. Expose the existing CLI and MCP with the command names supported at delivery time; preserve the current runtime requirements and project data contracts. Do not add a GUI or redesign other distribution channels. Resolve format-specific runtime, executable-path and sandbox limitations within this task. Reuse common application payload preparation, build/release tooling and application-owned install/update/uninstall logic across distribution channels and target builds. Do not create or copy separate implementations or scripts for each format, platform or release build. Keep only the final distribution artifacts and minimal format-required metadata/declarative packaging adapters channel-specific; delegate lifecycle operations to the native package manager or shared application mechanisms as appropriate.
acceptance: Build the MSI (.msi) artifact from the release candidate and make it available through the project's owner-approved release workflow; declare actual published-download verification as a read-only post-merge check.

On Windows x64, install the actual artifact using the native Windows package installer; from the documented user environment, verify the installed version, create/list tasks in a sample project and connect a fresh MCP client through the documented launch command.
Verify updating an older package to the candidate and reinstalling it preserve project records, IDs, unknown fields and project configuration; document any required runtime prerequisites.

Verify native removal cleans the channel's managed installation and command entries, preserves project/skill data and unrelated files, and follows the application's current cleanup contract. Verify interference with an existing installation is handled or clearly documented.
Add focused package lifecycle verification appropriate to this format and update the owning installation/release documentation. Record actual native evidence and explicit platform limitations.

Review the packaging paths to confirm they reuse common payload/build/release and application-owned lifecycle implementations. Format/platform differences are limited to final artifacts and necessary packaging metadata or thin adapters, with no duplicated build or install/update/uninstall scripts; native package-manager lifecycle behavior remains native. Verify this channel's actual artifact still passes its installed CLI/MCP and lifecycle acceptance.
